questions.question_text: The rate of depression in males is as much as in females in which of the following age groups?
questions.explanation: In pre -pubescent age group, the prevalence is up to 3% with 1:1 gender ratio. In adolescent age group the prevalence is 8% for males and 14% for females.

questions.question_text: Which mode of treatment is the mainstay in the management of encopresis?
questions.explanation: In most cases of encoperesis, considerable family discord and distress are common. It is important to reduce the family tensions about the symptom and a nonpunitive atmosphere is established. Education of the family and correction of misperceptions that a family may have about soiling must occur before treatment.A paediatric referral is always indicated. Behavioural methods are the mainstay of treatment and ongoing behavioural intervention to enhance appropriate bowel behaviour and diminish anxiety related to bowel movement.

questions.question_text: What genetic aetiology most increases the risk of the parents having a further child with Down's syndrome?
questions.explanation: In about 94% of cases, Down syndrome is caused by primary non -disjunction leading to Trisomy 21. The risk of recurrence of this abnormality is low if maternal age is also relatively low. But if there is Robertsonian translocation (eg 14:21), then risk of recurrence shoots up.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is not routinely recommended in the management of anxiety disorder in children and adolescents?
questions.explanation: If pharmacological treatment is required, then SSRIs are first -line agents. Overall, efficacy and safety data support the use of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) to treat childhood social phobia, Separation anxiety disorder and generalised anxiety disorder. Recent studies have demonstrated the efficacy of SSRIs for specific anxiety disorders. Benzodiazepines are not indicated as a routine treatment in children due to their potential adverse effects. There is also little or no evidence for the efficacy of other anxiolytics, such as buspirone or beta -blockers.

questions.question_text: The rate of self -harm in teenagers who identify with Goth culture is around
questions.explanation: Identification with the Goth youth subculture is strongly associated with self -harm and attempted suicide. A longitudinal cohort study by Young and colleagues of 1258 people aged 19 who had been followed up since they were 11, found that the prevalence of self -harm and attempted suicide were 53% and 47% respectively among the participants who identified most strongly with the Goth subculture. Prevalences of self -harm and attempted suicide in the whole sample were 7% and 6%. Young, R. et al. Prevalence of deliberate self -harm and attempted suicide within contemporary Goth youth subculture: longitudinal cohort study. BMJ 2006 332: 1058 -10

questions.question_text: In a child with developmental disturbances, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) study revealed hypoplasia of cerebellar vermis. The diagnosis is most likely to be
questions.explanation: Hypoplasia of cerebellar vermal lobules VI and VII, in addition to other cortical abnormalities, especially gyrification defects, have been observed in some autistic patients. Other MRI findings include increased brain size; increase in the size of the lateral and 4th ventricles; frontal lobe and cerebellar abnormalities. 'The greatest average percentage increase in size occurred in the occipital lobe, parietal lobe, and temporal lobe. No differences were found in the frontal lobes. The increased volume can arise from three different possible mechanisms: increased neurogenesis, decreased neuronal death, and increased production of nonneuronal brain tissue, such as Glial cells or blood vessels. Brain enlargement has been suggested as a possible biological marker for autistic disorder'. A pathological examination may reveal abnormal Purkinje cells in cerebellar vermis; abnormal limbic architecture (Excerpt retrieved from Kaplan & Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry 10th ed).

questions.question_text: Gilles de la Tourette syndrome is characterised by all except

options.text: Mean age of onset is seven years
Symptoms present for at least a year

questions.explanation: Gilles De La Tourette's syndrome is characterised by multiple motor and one or more vocal tics, present for at least a year, causing distress and impaired function. The onset is before age 18 years. Mean age of onset is 7 years and Male: Female ratio is 3:1.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following genetic disorders is closely associated with autism?
questions.explanation: Fragile X syndrome, a genetic disorder in which a portion of the X chromosome fractures, appears to be associated with autistic disorder. Approximately 1 -4 percent of children with autistic disorder also have fragile X syndrome. Tuberous sclerosis, a genetic disorder characterized by multiple benign tumours, with autosomal dominant transmission is also found with greater frequency among children with autistic disorder. Up to 2 percent of children with autistic disorder may also have tuberous sclerosis. Autistic disorder is also associated with neurological conditions, notably congenital rubella and phenylketonuria (PKU).

questions.question_text: In terms of treatments for children and adolescents with anorexia nervosa, which of the following treatments does a large body of evidence support?
questions.explanation: Family interventions that directly address the eating disorder are especially useful for children and adolescents with anorexia nervosa. (NICE Guidelines)

questions.question_text: The male to female ratio for conduct disorder is
questions.explanation: Estimated rates of conduct disorder among the general population range from 1 to 10 percent, with a general population rate of approximately 5 percent. The disorder is more common among boys than girls, and the male: female ratio is 4:1 (DSM -IV TR).

questions.question_text: A patient who is diagnosed with ADHD is found to have a comorbid bipolar disorder. All of the following symptoms could be explained by either diagnosis except
questions.explanation: Decreased need for sleep and lack of sleep is more closely associated with hypomania/mania of bipolar disorder. ADHD on its own does not produce sleeplessness.

questions.question_text: With respect to the delayed development of empathy skills which of the following is correct?

options.text: Most delayed in hearing children of hearing parents
Most delayed in deaf children of hearing parents
Most delayed in deaf children of deaf parents
Most delayed in hearing children of hearing parents
Most delayed in adopted children of deaf parents

correct_answer.text: Most delayed in deaf children of hearing parents

correct_answers.text: Most delayed in deaf children of hearing parents

questions.explanation: Deaf preadolescents have more difficulty with empathy development than hearing children, and this ability is related to the onset of deafness (Bachara, 1980). Deaf children born to deaf parents are better in the following areas compared to those born to hearing parents:1. maturity2. independence3. responsibility taking4. impulse control5. empathizing ability6. better match of parental expectations and achievements.Bachara, GH. Empathy development in deaf preadolescents. American Annals of the Deaf, 125; 38 -41 Feb 1980.Moores, DF and Meadow -Orlans, KP (ed). Educational and Developmental Aspects of Deafness. Gallaudet University Press 1990. Page 291 -93

questions.question_text: The condition commonly associated with autistic spectrum disorders is;
questions.explanation: Converging findings from clinic -based studies (Goldstein and Schwebach 2004) indicate that symptoms consistent with ADHD are present in a significant proportion of patients with autistic spectrum disorders anywhere between 50 -75%. Similarly, symptoms characteristic of autistic spectrum disorder have been observed in children who meet the criteria for ADHD.

questions.question_text: What is the chance of a 12 -year-old boy with conduct disorder developing antisocial personality disorder?
questions.explanation: Conduct disorder is often chronic and not amenable to treatment. Adult outcomes included antisocial personality disorder, criminality, substance misuse, and mental disorders. 50% of CD cases have severe persistent antisocial problems as adults.

questions.question_text: A 12 yr old boy is found to be skipping school repeatedly and using drugs with his friends. He is most likely to have which of the following diagnosable psychiatric conditions?
questions.explanation: Conduct disorder is an enduring set of antisocial and aggressive behaviours that evolves over time, usually characterized by aggression and violation of the rights of others.

questions.question_text: You are seeing a 2 -year-old boy in the clinic, whose vocabulary was limited to only four words (mama, daddy, hi, and more). He rarely communicated but used these words one at a time in appropriate situations. He supplemented his infrequent verbal communications with pointing and other simple gestures to request desired objects or actions. What would be the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Communication disorders Communication disorders are among the most common disorders in childhood. Language disorders include expressive and mixed receptive -expressive language disorder, whereas speech disorders include phonological disorder and stuttering. Expressive Language disorders Expressive language disorder is diagnosed when a child demonstrates a selective deficit in expressive language development relative to receptive language skills and nonverbal intelligence. A child with expressive language disorder is likely to function below the expected levels of acquired vocabulary, correct tense usage, complex sentence constructions, and word recall. A child with an expressive language disorder exhibits the following features: limited vocabulary, simple grammar, and variable articulation. Language understanding (decoding) skills remain relatively intact.

questions.question_text: The risk factors common to children and adolescents who attempt suicide includes all except
questions.explanation: Cognitive distortions characterized by hopelessness and helplessness are often noted in adolescents that attempt suicide.

questions.question_text: The most common co -morbid psychiatric disorder seen in children with ADHD is
questions.explanation: Co-morbid psychiatric illness is common in ADHD children and is seen in 50 -80% of cases. 50% children may meet criteria for 2 comorbid conditions. Oppositional Defiant disorder in 35 -50%, conduct disorder 25%, anxiety disorder 25% and depressive disorder 15%. Learning disability 15 -40%, specific language impairment in 15 -75% children.

questions.question_text: Which one among the following is NOT a core diagnostic feature of ADHD?
questions.explanation: Clinical features of ADHD: The cardinal features of ADHD are excessive and impairing levels of activity, inattention, and impulsiveness. Hyperactivity -impulsivity symptoms include fidgeting, moving, getting up and running about, talking excessively; unable to play quietly; continually interrupting. Inattention symptoms include: easily distracted, poor attention span and cannot sustain attention; poor task completion; can't organize, and makes mistakes with tasks that require attention; doesn't listen, is forgetful, and loses things for tasks.

questions.question_text: Children with enuresis have shown improvement with which one of the following antidepressant?
questions.explanation: Classic conditioning with the bell and pad apparatus is generally the most effective treatment for enuresis, with dryness resulting in more than 50 percent of cases. A star chart may be particularly helpful. Imipramine is efficacious and has been approved for use in treating childhood enuresis, primarily on a short -term basis. Desmopressin, an antidiuretic compound that is available as an intranasal spray, has shown some initial success in reducing enuresis.

questions.question_text: What is the common reason for parents and children to seek treatment for Separation anxiety disorder?
questions.explanation: Children with Separation anxiety disorder (SAD) show anxiety about actual or anticipated separation from or danger to attachment figure, sleep disturbances and nightmares, and repeated occurrence of physical symptoms that includes nausea, vomiting, headache, stomach aches etc especially on occasions that involves separation from a major attachment figure. The latter may be associated with school refusal (especially in adolescents)and is the most common reasons for parents and children to seek treatment for SAD.

questions.question_text: In early -onset variant of schizophrenia, the age of onset of symptoms is before
questions.explanation: Childhood -onset schizophrenia (COS) is a rare and severe form of schizophrenia characterized by an onset of psychotic symptoms by age 12 years, believed to represent a subgroup of affected individuals with an increased heritable etiology. The term early -onset schizophrenia is preferred if the- onset is between ages 12 and 18.

questions.question_text: Heller's syndrome is characterised by normal development until
questions.explanation: Childhood disintegrative disorder (CDD) also called Heller's syndrome, and disintegrative psychosis is characterized by a marked regression in several areas of functioning after at least 2 years of apparently normal development. There is normal development for 2 -3 years, followed by a loss of acquired motor, language, and social skills between ages 3 and 4 years.

questions.question_text: A 15-year-old boy has moderate depression and no suicidality. He is known to be a successful student at his school and has a stable family support. The most suitable first line treatment is
questions.explanation: CBT alone could be offered for this patient with moderate depression - no suicidal risk; refusal of which or failure may prompt use of SSRIs (in accordance with NICE). There is a certain conflict of best evidence and recommended practice in adolescent depression. NICE recommendations are diametrically different from results of TADS study. Treatment of Adolescents with Depression Study (TADS) is the only published study to compare CBT, fluoxetine, their combination, and placebo. CBT (43% significantly improved) was not superior to placebo (35%), whereas both combination (71%) including fluoxetine, and fluoxetine alone (61%), were markedly superior to both CBT and to placebo. The combination treatment (CBT + fluoxetine) showed a faster recovery than any of the other treatments. A possible explanation for the relatively weak performance of CBT in this study could be the nature of TADS treatment package, which attempted to deliver a large number of approaches such as problem solving, behaviour activation, cognitive restructuring, emotion regulation, relaxation training etc in a brief period.

questions.question_text: Which of the following scales could be used in epidemiological studies as a screening tool for caseness among school -going children before further diagnostic procedures?
questions.explanation: CBCL is not a general psychopathology screening tool. 'It is used as a device by which parents or other individuals who know the child well rate a child's problem behaviors and competencies. This instrument can either be self -administered or administered through an interview. The CBCL can also be used to measure a child's change in behavior over time or following a treatment'. The Infant -Toddler Social -Emotional Assessment (ITSEA) is a parent-completed questionnaire that takes approximately 30 min to complete. 'It assesses four broad symptom domains —externalising, internalising, dysregulation and competence —and generates three indices—maladaptive behaviours, atypical behaviours and social relatedness. The ITSEA is designed for ages 12 -36 months'. The Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ) 'is a widely researched 25-item rating scale for youth aged 3 -17 years. It addresses emotional symptoms, conduct problems, hyperactive/inattention, peer relationships and prosocial behaviour. The SDQ also includes functional impact questions to better discriminate clinical significance'.The General Health Questionnaire (GHQ) 'is a widely used self-administered questionnaire designed to screen for mental health problems in adults. The GHQ -36 assesses domains related to anxiety, depression, somatic symptoms and social dysfunction, and was found to be an effective screening tool in a Finnish epidemiological study'. The GHQ is recommended for subjects who are 19 and 21 years of age. SCQ Social communication questionnaire is used the in assessment of autistic spectrum disorders. Connor's scale is used in ADHD assessment.

questions.question_text: The onset of autistic spectrum disorder occurs generally before the age of
questions.explanation: By definition, the onset of the autistic disorder is before the age of 3 years, although, in some cases, it is not recognized until a child is much older. Autistic disorder is four to five times more frequent in boys than in girls.

questions.question_text: Miss. X is a 16 -year-old girl who was assessed in the CAMHS outpatient clinic and was diagnosed with Bulimia nervosa? Her mother wishes her daughter to have a psychotherapeutic intervention. Which one of the following is the most effective treatment in this age group?
questions.explanation: Bulimia nervosa in adolescents is most often treated effectively with CBT. CBT is the first -line treatment for bulimia nervosa. It has been found to be the most effective treatment in over 35 controlled studies. In these studies the treatment program was usually 16 -20 weeks, after which 40-50% of the patients were abstinent from both bingeing and purging. A reduction of bingeing and purging occurred in 70 -95% of patients. Another 30% of those who did not show improvement immediately after treatment did show improvement to full recovery one year after treatment.

questions.question_text: Which of the following sleep -related movement disorders is associated with the use of stimulants?
questions.explanation: Bruxism is associated with cocaine, amphetamines, alcohol ingestion and also SSRI use.

questions.question_text: The commonest blood picture expected in adolescents with anorexia nervosa is
questions.explanation: Blood picture in anorexia nervosa: Normocytic normochromic anaemia, Leucopenia and thrombocytopenia.

questions.question_text: A report card can be used as a tool in the treatment of which of the following disorders?
questions.explanation: Behavioral techniques such as learning to attend to a stimulus of interest and ignore disruptive behaviours can help those who suffer from ADHD. A report card can be used as an effective behavioural tool connecting school and home. It can be used as a reinforcer for behaviour.

questions.question_text: In autistic spectrum disorder, the symptom that does not improve over time is
questions.explanation: Autistic disorder is generally a lifelong disorder with an uncertain prognosis. Overall predictors of good prognosis are early speech acquisition by ages 5 to 7 years and high intelligence (IQs above 70). Most demonstrated positive changes in communication and social domains over time. The symptom areas that did not seem to improve over time were those related to ritualistic and repetitive behaviours. In general, adult -outcome studies indicate that about two -thirds of autistic adults remain severely handicapped and live in complete dependence or semi dependence, either with their relatives or in long-term institutions.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is listed in the ICD -10 criteria for a diagnosis of childhood autism?

options.text: A particular interest in collecting things
Reduced sharing of interests with others

correct_answer.text: Reduced sharing of interests with others

correct_answers.text: Reduced sharing of interests with others

questions.explanation: Autistic Disorder (historically called early infantile autism, childhood autism, or Kanner's autism) is characterized by symptoms from each of the following three categories: Qualitative impairment in social interaction, Impairment in communication [language delay is most common cause for initial referral] and Restricted repetitive and stereotyped patterns of behaviour or interests. By definition, the onset of the autistic disorder is before the age of 3 years, although, in some cases, it is not recognized until a child is much older. Autistic disorder is four to five times more frequent in boys than in girls. There has been an apparent increase in prevalence rates over the years.

questions.question_text: Which of the following symptoms is rare in early -onset schizophrenia?
questions.explanation: Auditory hallucinations commonly occur in children with schizophrenia. Visual hallucinations are also experienced by a significant number of children with schizophrenia and often are frightening. Blunted or inappropriate affects appear almost universally in children with schizophrenia. Children with schizophrenia may giggle inappropriately or cry without being able to explain why. Formal thought disorders, including loosening of associations and thought blocking, are common features among children with schizophrenia. Illogical thinking and poverty of thought are also often present. A catatonic presentation is uncommon in early onset variants.

questions.question_text: What is the medication of choice for an 8 -year-old child with ADHD and tics?
questions.explanation: Atomoxetine is an NA Reuptake inhibitor showing an efficacy that parallels methylphenidate. It may be useful where stimulants are abused or when tics are present; in addition, its once -daily dosing makes it convenient for school -going children.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the best -suited treatment option for a teenager with ongoing substance use and ADHD?
questions.explanation: Atomoxetine has no abuse potential, unlike the amphetamines. Appropriate treatment and response of severe ADHD symptoms can reduce the later risk of substance abuse.

questions.question_text: Asperger's syndrome is characterised by all except

options.text: Impaired intellectual ability and syntactical speech
Restricted but repetitive stereotyped patterns of behaviour, interests and activities
Lack of awareness of the feeling of others

correct_answer.text: Impaired intellectual ability and syntactical speech

correct_answers.text: Impaired intellectual ability and syntactical speech

questions.explanation: Asperger's syndrome is characterised by severe persistent impairment in social interactions, repetitive behaviour patterns, and restricted interests. IQ and language are normal. Unlike autistic disorder, in Asperger's disorder no significant delays occur in language, cognitive development, or age-appropriate self -help skills. The clinical features include at least two of the following feature s of qualitative social impairment: 'Abnormal nonverbal communicative gestures, the failure to develop peer relationships, the lack of social or emotional reciprocity, and an impaired ability to express pleasure in other persons' happiness. Restricted interests and patterns of behaviour are always present, but when they are subtle, they may not be immediately identified or singled out as different from those of other children' (ICD -10). Mild motor clumsiness and a family history of autism may be present.

questions.question_text: In early childhood, depression will manifest as clingy behaviour, school refusal and exaggerated fears. The percentage of adolescents up to 19 years of age who will have experienced a diagnosable episode of depression in the Europe is
questions.explanation: Around 20 -30% can have a diagnosable episode before age 19, but often these episodes are unattended and appear only in epidemiological surveys seeking lifetime prevalence.

questions.question_text: The most common adverse outcome of conduct disorder seen in adults is the development of which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation: Approximately 40 -50% of children with conduct disorders may develop antisocial personality disorder as adults.

questions.question_text: The common presentations of anxiety disorders in preschool children include
questions.explanation: Anxiety symptoms vary with age. Tearfulness and clinging in preschool children. Somatic complaints and hypochondriacal fretting are common in middle childhood (5 -12) as are irritability and aggressive behaviour. Separation anxiety disorder and specific phobia usually have onset in early childhood.

questions.question_text: Which of the following disorders is among the most common psychiatric presentations seen in the adolescents?
questions.explanation: Anxiety disorders are among the most common conditions affecting children and adolescents, with prevalence in the 4% to 20% range. They adversely impact self -esteem, social relationships, and academic performance.

questions.question_text: Select the adolescent -onset disorder for which social disadvantage is not an established risk factor
questions.explanation: Anorexia is commoner among upper social class, but social class bias may be modest, and social disadvantage is not a strong determinant (Kendell 1973).

questions.question_text: In PANDAS, Which of the following psychiatric symptoms is rare?
questions.explanation: In pandas (Pediatric Autoimmune Neuropsychiatric Disorders Associated with Streptococcal infections), auditory hallucinations are not a common feature.

questions.question_text: Seizures and irregular respiration are commonly associated features seen in
questions.explanation: An associated feature of Rett syndrome is irregular respiration, with episodes of hyperventilation, apnoea, and breath holding. The disorganized breathing occurs in most patients while they are awake; during sleep, the breathing usually normalizes. Many patients with Rett's disorder also have scoliosis and spasticity. Developmental arrest plateaus and many may reach adulthood although disability is severe and prognosis poor.

questions.question_text: Which of the following drugs has the most supportive evidence base for the treatment of obsessive -compulsive disorder in childhood?
questions.explanation: Amongst all antidepressants, Sertraline has the most supportive evidence base for the treatment of Obsessive -compulsive disorder (the Paediatric OCD Treatment Study - POTS).

questions.question_text: The onset of oppositional defiant disorder is generally between the ages
questions.explanation: Although the oppositional defiant disorder can begin as early as 3 years of age, it typically is noted by 8 years of age and usually not later than adolescence.

questions.question_text: The most important organic cause to be excluded for children with encopresis is
questions.explanation: Although encopresis is considered a nonorganic disorder, more than three -fourths of children with encopretic behaviour may show evidence of chronic constipation, leading to infrequent defecation, withholding of bowel movements, which then leads to impaction and eventual overflow soiling. However, it is important to exclude organic cause such as Hirschsprung's disease, anorectal pathology, neurological problems; nutritional disorders and medication -induced.

questions.question_text: The known risk factors for child abuse include all except

options.text: Parent figure who is biologically unrelated to the child
Parent who was abused as a child

questions.explanation: Although child abuse occurs at all socioeconomic levels, it is highly associated with poverty and psychosocial stress, especially financial stress. Child maltreatment is strongly correlated with less parental education, underemployment, poor housing, welfare reliance, and single parenting.

questions.question_text: Melatonin is considered to be an effective treatment for children with learning disabilities and sleep disorders. Which of the following significantly improves on treatment with this drug?
questions.explanation: All forms of insomnia are common in children with learning difficulties, autism, ADHD and sensory impairments (particularly visual). Although behavioural interventions should be the primary intervention and have a robust evidence base, exogenous melatonin is now the first line medication for childhood insomnia. It decreases the time taken to fall asleep (sleep latency). A meta -analytic study by Braam et al. showed that melatonin treatment decreased sleep latency by a mean of 34 minutes, increased total sleep time by a mean of 50 minutes and significantly reduced the number of wakes per night. (Ref: The Maudsley prescribing guidelines (pg 279) - 10th edition).

questions.question_text: According to DSM criteria, ADHD is present in what percentage of children?
questions.explanation: ADHD may affect as many as 10% of the population in the United States. Approximately 5% of children ages 9 to 17 are affected at any given time, and a possible 2 -4% of adults are affected. The occurrence of ADHD is reported worldwide; statistical variations may be due to cultural perceptions of behavior.

questions.question_text: Which of the following pharmacological options is suitable for the treatment of a girl with ADHD and frequent aggressive outbursts?
questions.explanation: ADHD and aggression: Atomoxetine unlikely beneficial; consider behavioural therapy; consider atypical antipsychotics, clonidine.

questions.question_text: What proportion of 15 to 16 -year-old adolescents admit to incidents of deliberate self-harm in the UK?
questions.explanation: Actual incidents of DSH are admitted by only 6.9% of adolescents. The prevalence of ideation is estimated to be far higher.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is not categorised as a pervasive developmental disorder?
questions.explanation: According to DSM -IV, PDDs include autism, Asperger's syndrome, Rett's syndrome, Childhood disintegrative disorder and PDD -Not Otherwise Specified. DSM -5 has dropped Asperger's syndrome, which is now brought under autistic spectrum disorders.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements regarding enuresis is true?

options.text: Behavioural treatments have no evidence base
Diagnosis can be made only after age 3

questions.explanation: A familial aggregation is noted for enuresis. Most children tend to remit spontaneously, provided they have a strong psychosocial makeup. Diagnosis can be only made after age 5. Urine alarm is a useful behavioural treatment. ADH in the form of vasopressin is a useful treatment.
